title: The Letters to the Seven Churches of Asia and Their Place in the Plan of the Apocalypse
author: W. M. Ramsay
summary: Classic archaeologist's study tying each letter to the geography, history and civic life of its city (Sardis' surprised acropolis, Philadelphia's earthquakes, Laodicea's wealth). Public domain.

title: The Letters to the Seven Churches of Asia in Their Local Setting
author: Colin J. Hemer
summary: The standard study of Revelation 2–3 against inscriptions, coins and archaeology; refines and sometimes corrects Ramsay's local allusions. Eerdmans reprint 2000.

title: Imperial Cults and the Apocalypse of John: Reading Revelation in the Ruins
author: Steven J. Friesen
summary: Archaeological and textual study of the imperial cults of Roman Asia (Pergamum, Smyrna, Ephesus) and how they illuminate John's critique of empire.

title: Revelation: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary (Anchor Yale Bible 38A)
author: Craig R. Koester
summary: Major critical commentary attentive to social, economic and religious setting and to the book's history of interpretation and influence.

title: The Lukewarmness of Laodicea (Revelation 3:16)
author: M. J. S. Rudwick
summary: Tyndale Bulletin 3. Argues 'hot' and 'cold' are both commendable (healing hot springs of Hierapolis, refreshing cold water) and 'lukewarm' alludes to Laodicea's tepid, mineral-laden aqueduct water; developed with E. M. B. Green in Expository Times.

title: Why the Laodiceans Received Lukewarm Water (Revelation 3:15-18)
author: Stanley E. Porter
summary: Tyndale Bulletin 38. Reviews the Rudwick–Green and Hemer case on Laodicea's water supply and its bearing on the 'lukewarm' image.

title: The Apocalyptic Imagination: An Introduction to Jewish Apocalyptic Literature
author: John J. Collins
summary: Standard introduction to the apocalypse genre (Daniel, 1 Enoch, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch and others), including the widely used SBL genre definition.
note: Well-known standard work; no URL checked during research.

title: The Book of Revelation (NICNT, revised)
author: Robert H. Mounce
summary: Evangelical commentary; late date, apostolic authorship held as probable, a blend of preterist setting and future consummation.

title: Revelation 1–7: An Exegetical Commentary
author: Robert L. Thomas
summary: Detailed dispensational futurist commentary; defends apostolic authorship, a late date and a pretribulational reading of Revelation 3:10.

title: A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Revelation of St. John (ICC, 2 vols.)
author: R. H. Charles
summary: Older critical commentary strong on Jewish apocalyptic parallels and Revelation's Semitic Greek; attributes the book to a John other than the apostle.
note: Public-domain work; no URL checked during research.

title: Redating the New Testament
author: John A. T. Robinson
summary: A liberal-critical scholar's argument that every New Testament book, Revelation included, was written before 70; dates Revelation to c. 68–70.

title: The Book of Revelation: Apocalypse and Empire
author: Leonard L. Thompson
summary: Argues the evidence for a Domitianic empire-wide persecution is thin and that Revelation addresses a perceived crisis of social accommodation rather than state terror.

title: Eusebius, Church History 3.18 and 5.8 (quoting Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3), NPNF series 2 vol. 1
author: Eusebius of Caesarea (trans. A. C. McGiffert, ed. P. Schaff)
summary: Public-domain translation of Eusebius, who preserves Irenaeus' Greek on when the Apocalypse 'was seen' (towards the end of Domitian's reign) and records Dionysius of Alexandria on its authorship.
